name: Matthew Johnson
headline: Automation Manager at Shaw Industries
icp_read: Large textile/flooring manufacturer (10k+ employees, Dalton GA). Automation Manager who owns floor automation, OEE, and data visibility across plants. Prior background at Tier 1 auto suppliers (AAM, Sejong) means he has brownfield muscle memory.
why_now: Answered a PLC SFC troubleshooting question with a practical check-the-i/o answer, signaling he debugs these problems hands-on. As Automation Manager at a large manufacturer who promoted from Maintenance Engineer through Automation Engineer, he is the decision-maker and implementer in one. Shaw has multiple large carpet/flooring plants; machine data visibility across those sites is a natural fit for SHARC (analog/discrete signal capture without PLC program changes) and DIME (data aggregation).
signal: Just checking the i/o that's not letting step1 enable
suggested_opener: At a plant like Shaw, what does your machine data collection look like beyond the PLC program - historian integration, or are you mostly reading tags directly out of the controller?

name: Saif Ghouse
headline: Lead Automation and Process Control Engineer at DuPont
icp_read: Large chemical/materials manufacturer. 25+ years combined Dow/DuPont. Currently leading control platform migrations (Rockwell PlantPax, ACM) at DuPont, Greater Chicago Area. OT brownfield migration work every day.
why_now: His signal on the SFC troubleshooting post was a teaching moment: he reframed the diagnostic question before answering it. He leads LOPA and PlantPax migrations - the exact moment when plants need to standardize their connectivity and historian layers. DIME reads natively from Rockwell EtherNet-IP without requiring program changes, which fits directly into what he does during migrations.
signal: If I use this as a teaching moment to a mentee, I would ask what am I troubleshooting? We're assuming failure to make the transition, but is that actually the desired action?
suggested_opener: Your 'what are we actually troubleshooting' framing on the SFC post is the right starting question. On the PlantPax migrations you're leading at DuPont - does the plant have a standard historian/OPC layer, or does each site wire it up differently?

name: Steffen Treutlein
headline: Manufacturing Manager (Tooling & Die Manufacturing) at Hirschvogel Components Mexico
icp_read: Automotive forging supplier (motor vehicle manufacturing, 501-1000 employees, San Juan del Rio Mexico). Runs a 40+ person tooling & die manufacturing department. Increased output 4x in 3 years through process discipline and data-driven decisions. Lean Six Sigma Black Belt. Parent Hirschvogel is a Tier 1 auto supplier.
why_now: Authored a post comparing Germany vs. Mexico manufacturing culture, signaling he thinks actively about operational systems. His About explicitly calls out data-driven decision making. A tooling & die department that grew from 400 to 1700 tools/month is producing machine-level activity that would benefit from utilization tracking - exactly what SHARC captures at the signal level without touching the PLC program. DISTANCE_3 means cold approach.
signal: Authored post on Germany vs. Mexico manufacturing culture differences and operational discipline
suggested_opener: Your Germany vs. Mexico post got me thinking about tooling ops specifically - at Hirschvogel, are you pulling machine utilization data off the tooling equipment, or is most of the output tracking still manual?

name: Dennis Strack
headline: Fabrications Manager at KION North America
icp_read: Discrete machinery manufacturer (forklift/industrial trucks, 201-500 employees, Summerville SC). Fabrications Manager overseeing welding, cutting, and forming operations. 30 years at Caterpillar as Manufacturing Operations Manager and Fabrications Manager before joining KION. Navy veteran.
why_now: A fabrications manager at a machinery manufacturer owns exactly the equipment where SHARC delivers fastest ROI: welders, plasma/laser cutters, press brakes, and other high-energy discrete machinery where signal-level utilization data is unavailable from the PLC program. His 30 years at Caterpillar means he has seen every generation of brownfield equipment and knows the pain of undocumented machines. OUT_OF_NETWORK means cold approach needed.
signal: Now I know why the strongbacks are so critical (comment on Columbia-class submarine bow dome construction photo at Newport News Shipbuilding)
suggested_opener: Thirty years of fabrication ops at Caterpillar before KION - on the fabrication floor there, are you getting machine utilization data off the welders and cutting equipment, or is it still mostly production counts from the PLC?

name: Andrew Schulman
headline: CEO / Industrial Automation Engineer at Schulman Engineering
icp_read: Small SI (2-10 employees, Westlake Village CA). Codesys enthusiast and Allen-Bradley practitioner doing industrial automation integration. Founded 2022. DISTANCE_1 - warmest path, can message directly.
why_now: His signal on the PLC post was actively curious about which platform the SFC was written in. Codesys plus Allen-Bradley experience in his headline means he handles mixed-platform brownfield environments. DIME speaks Codesys/ADS natively alongside Rockwell EtherNet-IP, which would be directly useful on mixed-vendor sites. DISTANCE_1 means he can be messaged without a connection request first.
signal: What software is this in, out of curiosity?
suggested_opener: Curious what your client platform spread looks like at Schulman - whether you're mostly on Codesys-based controllers or dealing with mixed Allen-Bradley / Siemens environments on the same site.

name: Steve Dobson, P.E.
headline: Chairman at TechVisor Group / iiOTec, Inc.
icp_read: Aggregating solo and small automation integrators into a consolidated platform (Green Bay WI). iiOTec is the foundational platform. Three acquisitions in motion. Member firms serve manufacturing, food & beverage, material handling clients.
why_now: He is building an integration roll-up. If TechVisor standardizes on a brownfield connectivity stack across its integrator network, a single adoption decision reaches multiple firms and their clients. He still engages at the controls level (his PLC comment was precise). DIME or SHARC as a standard tool across TechVisor member firms would be a channel multiplier - one conversation that touches several deployments.
signal: All of those need to = 1. Put your mouse over each one individually and see which of them are not 1.
suggested_opener: The TechVisor roll-up model is interesting - do the integrators you're bringing in share a common stack for protocol connectivity on client sites, or is it rebuilt per project?

name: Jimmy DiTraglia
headline: Owner - JD Controls LLC | Automation Controls Engineer
icp_read: Solo controls engineering firm (0-1 employees, Simpsonville SC, founded June 2024). 14 years experience across food & beverage, conveyance, packaging, natural gas processing, chemical process, robotics. Allen-Bradley and TwinCAT 3 experience.
why_now: Freshly independent for one year. His SFC comment was the most technically detailed of any commenter - he named exactly what to look at (transition tags), referenced Rockwell SFC behavior specifically, and has both Allen-Bradley and Beckhoff (TwinCAT 3) platform experience. A solo integrator without hardware capital is exactly the profile SHARC and DIME serve: he can deploy brownfield connectivity on a client site in hours and bill it as a deliverable without floating PO capital.
signal: Program is being called, hence the green outline on Step_000. Switch the view to see the online values, then you'd know which condition(s) are not being met to move into Step_001.
suggested_opener: For your food & bev and packaging work at JD Controls - do your clients typically give you access to the PLC program for data extraction, or are you often working around restricted ladder logic on older installs?

name: John Tarter
headline: Founder at QED Automation LLC | Automation Systems Fixer
icp_read: Custom automation firm (2-10 employees, Henderson NV, founded 2018). Called in when systems pass development but break in production. Background in medical device, semiconductor, energy, and industrial automation. Delivers full systems from concept through commissioning.
why_now: His positioning is explicitly 'I get pulled in when it is broken.' His listed failure modes: systems that work in development but fall apart in production, integration issues across mechanical, controls, and software. That is often a connectivity problem, not a logic problem. His skeptical comment on the bakery post showed he critically evaluates automation claims - he will appreciate a practitioner framing over a product pitch.
signal: Not really sure I believe the pretzel twisting thing. Done work in baked product production and seems really slow. Is this a real example of a real executed process?
suggested_opener: When you're called in to stabilize systems that passed development but fall apart in production - is the failure usually in the control logic, the sensor layer, or the handoff between the control system and data infrastructure?

name: Alex Marcy
headline: CEO at Corso Systems | Industrial Automation SI
icp_read: Manufacturing SI (11-50 employees, Chicago, founded 2011). Specialties: PLC programming, HMI/SCADA, MES, IIoT, Ignition, Unified Namespace, Industry 4.0. PE license 2010. Built Corso from scratch over 14 years serving manufacturing clients.
why_now: Active SI doing brownfield connectivity and data integration for manufacturers. His authored post on RFP confusion signals he is actively winning new manufacturing automation projects. Ignition shop doing IIoT work - on brownfield sites where legacy controllers do not speak OPC-UA natively, DIME handles protocol translation without custom code and slots directly into their deployment stack. CEO with technical PE background means he makes tooling decisions.
signal: Authored post complaining about a confusing amendment-heavy RFP in industrial automation bidding
suggested_opener: Corso has been at this 14 years - on brownfield deployments where the legacy controllers do not have native OPC-UA, what is your current go-to for the connectivity layer before Ignition?

name: Jim Bercik
headline: VP of Sales and Marketing at Southern Flow, Inc.
icp_read: SCADA/PLC/HMI/panel fabrication SI (11-50 employees, Alpharetta GA). Specialties: PLC programming, HMI, high-performance SCADA graphics, panel fabrication, instrument calibration, field service. VP Sales spent 20+ years at MR Systems (automation integrator) before Southern Flow.
why_now: His comment on the digital transformation post hit the execution accountability gap directly: who owns the connectivity and integration work once the project is sold. That is where DIME removes friction - the protocol driver runs without a dedicated owner writing custom code. His VP Sales role means he sees the project lifecycle from proposal to delivery and can influence which tools the team standardizes on.
signal: The missing question is often who owns execution, and when does it begin (comment on Dylan DuFresne digital transformation post)
suggested_opener: Your execution ownership point on Dylan's post is the right question - at Southern Flow, once a connectivity or historian project is sold, who actually owns the protocol layer day-to-day through delivery?

name: Dustin Symes
headline: CTO at JPI Solutions | SCADA, IIoT, OT/IT Convergence
icp_read: SCADA/IIoT integrator (11-50 employees, Calgary AB). Specialties: SCADA, IIoT, automation, DCS, PLC, HMI, digital transformation, OT/IT convergence. Serves oil & gas, mining, and manufacturing. CTO sets technical direction and tooling decisions for the firm.
why_now: Canadian SI doing OT/IT convergence with brownfield equipment across oil & gas and manufacturing. DIME and SHARC are useful anywhere Modbus, DNP3, or legacy industrial protocols surface - common across oil & gas field equipment. CTO role means he makes or directly influences stack decisions. Signal is weak (personal post) but role alignment is strong.
signal: Feed post about new Framework laptop (off-topic personal post; role and company are on-target)
suggested_opener: JPI does OT/IT convergence across oil & gas and manufacturing - on brownfield retrofits, what protocols are you hitting most often where connectivity is still the bottleneck?

name: Rick Bullotta
headline: Advisor / Investor / Mentor | IIoT and Industrial Software Ecosystem
company: Various (HighByte, Tulip, TwinThread, InfluxData, OpsmateAI, Losant)
icp_read: IIoT ecosystem insider. Founded Lighthammer (acquired by SAP 2003) and ThingWorx (acquired by PTC 2013). Currently advising and investing in HighByte (industrial data ops), Tulip (manufacturing operations platform), TwinThread (industrial intelligence), InfluxData (time series DB), OpsmateAI, Losant. Deep rolodex across the IIoT vendor space.

His portfolio companies (HighByte, TwinThread) are data infrastructure plays where DIME and SHARC fill the edge connectivity gap. His pragmatic signal - results over methodology - aligns with Chris's signal-level bypass philosophy. A connection here is a peer and network play, not a direct product sale.
signal: Well, if tablets running Excel delivers the results, who cares? (comment on industrial automation ROI discussion at Abelara/Dylan DuFresne post)
suggested_opener: Your tablets-running-Excel take is a useful gut check against IIoT theater. In the companies you are advising now - where does the brownfield connectivity layer still cause the most integration pain?
